column2: On the authority of the Commander of the Believers, Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Actions are only by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended.

So whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated.” Agreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim).
Innamā (“only”): for restriction, which is affirming the ruling for what is mentioned and negating it for everything else.
Al-aʿmāl (“actions”): bodily acts, both words and deeds, that require an intention.
Al-niyyāt (“intentions”): plural of niyyah; linguistically it means aim, and in the Sharīʿah, the heart's resolve to do something, joined with doing it. Imriʾ (“person”): an individual.
Mā nawā (“what he intended”): what he aimed at, whether good or evil.

Al-hijrah (“emigration”): linguistically, leaving; in the Sharīʿah, moving from a land of shirk to a land of Islam, or from a land of sins to a land of uprightness. Yuṣībuhā (“he would attain it”): he would obtain it.

Dunyā (“worldly gain”): what is on the face of the earth, together with the air and the atmosphere; what is meant here is wealth specifically. It is called dunyā because it is near (danā) to passing away, or because it comes before the Hereafter. Yankiḥuhā (“he would marry her”): he would take her as a wife.
Ilā mā hājara ilayh (“to that for which he emigrated”): whatever he aimed at, whether worldly gain, a woman or something else.
In the gloss on dunyā the printed text reads الهوى (desire), evidently for الهواء (the air), as in al-Tuḥfah al-Rabbāniyyah.
It is not permissible to undertake any deed until one knows its ruling.
Delegation is not permissible in the intention itself.
A deed is not valid from someone heedless of the intention, and no deed prescribed by the Sharīʿah counts without an intention.
Performing acts of worship on another's behalf is not permissible, except where a proof makes an exception.
The virtue of emigrating from a land of shirk to a land of Islam, seeking the pleasure of Allah the Exalted, or from a land in which sins are committed to a land whose people are upright.
Sincerity in deeds for Allah the Exalted, and wariness of showing off (riyāʾ), seeking reputation (sumʿah), and working for the sake of this world.
The place of the intention is the heart, and pronouncing it is an innovation.

This hadith is one of the great principles of the religion, of lofty standing and abundant benefit, because it is one of the comprehensive hadiths around which Islam revolves. In this hadith the Messenger ﷺ made clear that all deeds prescribed by the Sharīʿah that require an intention, whether words or actions, coming from any believer, are neither valid nor accepted without the intention,
because the intention is the foundation and the measure of all deeds and words.

If the intention is sound, the deed is sound, and if it is corrupt, the deed is corrupt. If the intention is righteous and the deed conforms to the Sharīʿah, the deed is accepted; but if something else is intended by it, the deed is rejected.
Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set this out in detail in this hadith
The printed text reads ثم إنا لرسول الله, evidently for ثم إن رسول الله (“Then the Messenger of Allah”).
with an example: whoever emigrates to the land of Islam out of love for Allah the Exalted and out of desire for Islam, to learn the religion and act upon it, obtains the reward of what he intended.

But if his aim and purpose are worldly matters, such as some worldly gain he would attain or a woman he would marry, his recompense is according to his aims. Allah, Glorified is He, knows the secret and what is yet more hidden, and He will recompense every doer for his deed: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.
When you make some good deed public, / let what you keep secret be better still.
For the one who hides good is marked by it, / and the one who hides evil is marked by evil.
Another poet:
A man who buys this world at the price of his religion / will leave it with a losing bargain.
Another poet:
If you must busy yourself with something, then do not / be busy with anything but what pleases Allah.
For nothing will accompany a person, before his death / or after it, except what he used to do.
